title: The Boycott
subtitle: Three Years of Siege in the Ravine of Abu Talib
summary: Quraysh's formal decree to ostracize Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib, the severe physical and economic isolation in Shi'b Abi Talib, the steadfast solidarity of the clan, the courageous coalition that broke the unjust parchment, and the termites that spared only the name of God.

sections.text: The rapid growth of Islam following the conversions of Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Umar ibn al-Khattab, coupled with the sanctuary enjoyed by the Muslim emigrants in Abyssinia, filled the leadership of Quraysh with profound anxiety. Their traditional methods of ridicule, theological debate, and localized torture had failed to arrest the movement's momentum. Meeting in the aristocratic council of Dar al-Nadwah in the seventh year of Prophethood, the chieftains resolved to implement an extreme collective punishment that defied Arab customary norms: total social and economic ostracism.

Under the leadership of Abu Jahl and other hardliners, a formal contract was drafted by Mansur ibn Ikrimah. The terms were uncompromising: no clan in Makkah would marry from Banu Hashim or Banu al-Muttalib, nor give their daughters to them in marriage; no merchant would buy from them or sell to them; and no social contact or reconciliation would be permitted until they unconditionally surrendered Muhammad ﷺ to be executed. To endow the pact with inviolable sanctity, the document was solemnly suspended inside the inner sanctum of the Kaaba.
The barren desert caravans and rugged passes where all commerce was denied to the besieged clans.

Faced with this draconian ultimatum, Abu Talib refused to abandon his nephew. With remarkable clan loyalty, he gathered the entirety of Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib—both those who had embraced Islam and those who still followed traditional paganism—and withdrew into a narrow mountain pass on the outskirts of Makkah known as Shi'b Abi Talib. Only one prominent family member broke rank: Abu Lahab, who abandoned his kin to ally openly with their persecutors.

The siege lasted for nearly three agonizing years, from the seventh to the tenth year of Prophethood. The physical toll was devastating. Whenever trading caravans arrived in Makkah during the sacred pilgrimage months, Abu Jahl and his confederates intercepted the merchants, offering exorbitant prices to buy up all provisions so that the besieged clans could purchase nothing. Deprived of basic sustenance, the families were reduced to chewing dry hides and boiling the bitter leaves of desert thorn trees (talh and samur). Classical chroniclers record that the agonizing cries of starving infants could be heard from across the valley of Makkah, troubling the conscience of fair-minded observers.

Despite the strict guard placed around the defile, secret acts of human decency breached the blockade. Men with maternal ties to Banu Hashim risked severe retaliation to smuggle food. Hakim ibn Hizam, nephew of Khadijah رضي الله عنها, repeatedly loaded camels with wheat and sent them driving into the ravine by night. Hisham ibn Amr of Banu Amir similarly loaded his beasts with provisions, brought them to the mouth of the defile, and drove them into the gorge to bring relief to the suffering families.

By the tenth year of Prophethood, moral revulsion against the merciless blockade began to crystallize into organized resistance. Hisham ibn Amr approached Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah, whose mother Atikah was the daughter of Abd al-Muttalib, appealing to his familial honor: 'O Zuhayr, are you content to eat fine food, wear fine robes, and marry women, while your uncles and kin are perishing in the defile, unable to trade or marry?' Stirred to action, Zuhayr agreed, but insisted that they needed allies.

Hisham methodically recruited three other influential noblemen: Mut'im ibn Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, and Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad. Meeting secretly by night on the upper slopes of Mount Hajjun, the five conspirators swore a mutual pact to stand together at the Kaaba the following morning and demand the immediate nullification of the unjust scroll.
The mountain slopes of Makkah where the alliance of conscience met under the cover of night.

At sunrise, the five leaders entered the courtyard of the Kaaba where the chiefs of Quraysh sat assembled. Zuhayr circled the sanctuary seven times, then stood before the gathered nobles and raised his voice: 'O people of Makkah! Do we eat food and wear fine clothes while Banu Hashim perish, unable to buy or sell? By God, I shall not sit down until this severing, unjust parchment is torn to shreds!'

Abu Jahl rose in outrage from his corner, shouting: 'You lie! By God, it shall not be torn!' Immediately, Zam'ah cried out: 'You lie more, by God! We were not pleased with it when it was written!' Abu al-Bakhtari and Mut'im ibn Adi echoed the denunciation in rapid succession, showing that this was no solitary protest but a concerted revolt of tribal conscience. Abu Jahl fell back in confusion, realizing that the matter had been prearranged under cover of darkness.

What follows is the account in Ibn Ishaq, not a report in the two Sahihs. At that juncture Abu Talib entered the sanctuary and said that his nephew had told him that termites had attacked the hanging document, consuming every word of injustice, severed kinship, and oppression, leaving intact only the name of God: 'Bismikallahumma' (In Your Name, O God). Abu Talib challenged the assembly: 'If my nephew's words are true, end your boycott; and if he is lying, I will surrender him to you.'

Mut'im ibn Adi stepped forward to fetch the parchment from the interior of the Kaaba. In that sirah account, when they unfurled the leaf they found it eaten, with nothing of the writing left except the words 'In Your name, O God.' The chapter does not present the termite report as an authenticated hadith. Confounded and humiliated, the hardliners had no recourse left. The five chieftains took up their weapons, escorted Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib out of the mountain pass, and brought the three-year siege to a permanent end.

The boycott of Banu Hashim revealed the moral bankruptcy of tribal tyranny when pitted against spiritual conviction and noble conscience. Though the siege ended in triumph, its severe physical privations had permanently weakened the elders of the clan, casting an ominous shadow over the monumental trials that lay ahead.
